author: Caroline Ann Bowles
poem_text_en:
River, river, little river!
Bright you sparkle on your way;
O’er the yellow pebbles dancing,
Through the flowers and foliage glancing,
Like a child at play.

River, river! Swelling river!
On you rush through rough and smooth;
Louder, faster, brawling, leaping.
Over rocks, by rose-banks, sweeping
Like impetuous youth.

River, river! Brimming river!
Broad and deep, and still as time;
Seeming still, yet still in motion,
Tending onward to the ocean,
Just like mortal prime.

River, river! Headlong river!
Down you dash into the sea,
Sea that line hath never sounded,
Sea that sail hath never rounded,
Like eternity.
summary_en: Caroline Ann Bowles compares the life of a river to the different stages of human life. From the playful childhood and impetuous youth to the mature prime and final eternity, the poem illustrates the river's journey as a reflection of man's growth and eventual transition to the unknown.

figures_of_speech.note_en: Comparing the movement of the river to a child.
Comparing the river's rush to the energy of youth.
Comparing the sea to the concept of eternity.

figures_of_speech.note_en: Repetition of 'Sea that' at the beginning of successive lines.

rules.rule_en: Caroline Ann Bowles (1786-1854) was the wife of poet laureate Robert Southey.
The poem uses a four-stanza structure to map the river's journey to human life stages.
The poem contains imagery like 'yellow pebbles' and 'rose-banks'.
